title: Weather and Seasons
bigQuestion: What is the weather doing today, and what pattern is it part of?

story.title: A Month of Stickers
story.kicker: Every morning our class puts one sticker on the weather chart. What will the chart show after thirty days?
paragraphs: Every morning, Mr. Ortiz's class looks out the window. Is it sunny? Is it cloudy? Is it raining? One student picks a sticker. A yellow sun. A gray cloud. A blue raindrop. A white snowflake. The student sticks it on today's square of the chart.

At first the chart was empty. Then the stickers grew. One week had four sun stickers. Another week had three rain stickers in a row. Everyone wore boots that week. The floor by the door was full of puddles.

After thirty days, the class counted. Twelve suns. Nine clouds. Six raindrops. Three snowflakes. Ana said, 'It was mostly sunny.' Jamal said, 'But it rained a lot too.' They were both right. The chart showed it.
A chart turns thirty days of looking into one picture. Scientists who study weather do the same thing. They look every day. They write it down. Then they look for patterns. So can you.
story.think: What would you want to count on a weather chart? Why would that be useful?

lessons.title: Look Out the Window
lessons.mainIdea: Weather is what the air outside is like right now.
reading: Step outside. What do you feel? Maybe the sun is warm on your face. Maybe cold wind pushes your hair. Maybe rain drips on your nose. All of that is *weather*. Weather is what the air is like today.
Weather can change fast. It can be sunny at lunch. It can be rainy at bedtime. That is why we look every day. Looking is the first job of a scientist.

words.d: what the air outside is like right now: sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, windy, hot or cold

look.title: One Morning, Two Ways
look.text: Picture a morning. The sky is blue. The sun shines on the sidewalk. Now picture another morning. The sky is gray. Water drips from the roof. Puddles cover the sidewalk.
look.prompt: What is the same on both mornings? What is different?

check.q: What is weather?
choices: What the air is like today
check.why: Weather is what the air outside is like right now.

check.q: Can weather change during one day?
choices: No, it stays the same all day
check.why: It can be sunny at lunch and rainy at bedtime. Weather can change fast.

check.q: What is a scientist's first job with weather?
check.why: Scientists look first. Looking every day is how they learn.

lessons.title: Kinds of Weather
lessons.mainIdea: Sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy and windy are kinds of weather.
reading: On a *sunny* day, the sky is clear. You can see the sun. On a *cloudy* day, clouds cover the sky. The sky looks gray or white.
On a rainy day, water falls from the clouds. On a snowy day, the water falls as soft white flakes. That happens when the air is very cold.
On a windy day, the air moves fast. You cannot see wind. But you see what it does. Flags flap. Leaves fly. Hats blow off.

words.d: a day with a clear sky and the sun shining
a day when clouds cover the sky

look.title: How Do You Know It Is Windy?
look.text: Look at the playground. The flag is standing straight out. The swings move with no one on them. A paper cup rolls across the ground. Nobody is touching any of it.
look.prompt: What is moving these things? How can you tell, even though you cannot see it?

check.q: What falls on a snowy day?
check.why: Snow is water that falls as soft white flakes.

check.q: You cannot see wind. How can you tell it is windy?
choices: You can see what wind does
check.why: Flags flap and leaves fly. We see what the wind does.

check.q: Snow falls when the air is...
check.why: Snow needs very cold air. Warm air gives rain.

lessons.title: Hot or Cold?
lessons.mainIdea: A thermometer measures how hot or cold the air is.
reading: Is it hot today? Is it cold? Your skin can tell you a little. A *thermometer* can tell you a number. The number is the *temperature*. It tells how warm the air is.
Many thermometers have a red line. When the air gets warmer, the line goes up. When the air gets colder, the line goes down. We read the number next to the line.
In Chicago, a winter day may be about 30 degrees. A summer day may be about 85 degrees. A bigger number means warmer air.

words.d: a tool that measures how hot or cold something is
how hot or cold something is, shown as a number

look.title: Chicago: How Warm Is a Day?
look.cite: NOAA climate normals for Chicago, rounded
look.prompt: Which month is warmest? Which is coldest? What would you wear in each?

check.q: What does a thermometer measure?
choices: How hot or cold it is
check.why: A thermometer gives a number for how hot or cold the air is.

check.q: The red line goes up. What does that mean?
check.why: The line goes up when the air gets warmer.

check.q: Which number means a warmer day?
check.why: A bigger number means warmer air. 85 is bigger than 30.

lessons.title: Our Weather Chart
lessons.mainIdea: A chart helps us count the weather and see patterns.
reading: One day of weather is easy to remember. Thirty days is hard. So we make a *chart*. Each day gets a picture. A sun. A cloud. A raindrop. A snowflake.
At the end of the month, we count. How many suns? How many clouds? Counting turns looking into numbers. Numbers help us compare.
Then we look for a *pattern*. Maybe January had many snow days. Maybe May had many rain days. A pattern is something that happens again and again.

words.d: a page where we record something each day so we can count it later
something that happens again and again in the same way

look.title: One Month of Stickers
look.cite: the class chart from our story (an example)
look.prompt: Which weather happened most? How many days had rain or snow together?

check.q: Why do we make a weather chart?
choices: To count weather and find patterns
check.why: A chart lets us count and see patterns over many days.

check.q: The chart has twelve suns and six raindrops. Which happened more?
check.why: Twelve is more than six. There were more sunny days.

check.q: What is a pattern?
choices: Something that happens again and again
check.why: A pattern repeats. It happens again and again.

lessons.title: Four Seasons in Illinois
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has four seasons, and each one has its own weather.
reading: Illinois has four *seasons*. Winter is cold. Snow may fall. Spring is cool and wet. Plants start to grow. Summer is hot. Fall is cool again. Leaves turn red and gold.
The seasons come in the same order every year. Winter, spring, summer, fall. Then winter again. That is a pattern too. A very big one.
Not every place has the same seasons. But in Illinois, we get all four. Each one brings its own kind of weather.

words.d: one of the four parts of the year: winter, spring, summer and fall

look.title: Same Tree, Four Times
look.text: Picture one tree in a yard. In winter its branches are bare and snow sits on them. In spring small green leaves pop out. In summer the tree is full and shady. In fall the leaves turn orange and drop.
look.prompt: Which season is the tree in right now where you live? How do you know?

check.q: How many seasons does Illinois have?
check.why: Illinois has four seasons: winter, spring, summer and fall.

check.q: Which season comes after summer?
check.why: The order is winter, spring, summer, fall. Fall comes after summer.

check.q: In which season does snow fall most in Illinois?
check.why: Winter is cold, and that is when snow falls.

lessons.title: Long Days, Short Days
lessons.mainIdea: Summer days have more daylight than winter days.
reading: In summer, the sun comes up early. It stays out late. You can play outside after dinner. In winter, the sun comes up late. It sets before dinner.
The amount of *daylight* changes with the seasons. Chicago gets about 15 hours of daylight in June. It gets about 9 hours in December. That is a big difference.
More daylight means more sun time. The sun warms the ground longer. That is one reason summer is hot. It is one reason winter is cold.

words.d: the time of day when the sun is up and the sky is bright

look.title: Daylight in Chicago
look.cite: standard sunrise and sunset tables for Chicago, rounded
look.prompt: Which month has the most daylight? Which has the least?

check.q: Which month has the most daylight in Chicago?
check.why: June has about 15 hours of daylight. That is the most.

check.q: In winter, when does the sun set?
check.why: Winter days are short. The sun sets early.

check.q: Why is summer warm?
choices: The sun is up longer and warms the ground more
check.why: More daylight means more time for the sun to warm the ground.

lessons.title: Big Weather, Get Ready
lessons.mainIdea: Some weather is dangerous, and forecasts help people get ready.
reading: Most weather is safe. Some weather is not. A *tornado* is a spinning wind that can knock down houses. A big snowstorm can block roads. A thunderstorm can bring lightning.
Weather scientists watch the sky and make a *forecast*. A forecast says what the weather will probably be. If a storm is coming, people can get ready.
At school, we practice a tornado drill. We go to a safe hall. We crouch down and cover our heads. On a big snow day, school may close. Forecasts help grown-ups decide.

words.d: a strong spinning wind that reaches down from a storm cloud
what weather scientists think the weather will be

look.title: The Sky Turns Dark
look.text: It is afternoon. The sky turns dark and strange. The wind picks up. A siren begins to wail across town. On the radio, a voice says a tornado warning is on. The teacher says, 'Line up. We are going to the hall.'
look.prompt: What should the students do next? Why is the hall safer than a room with big windows?

check.q: What does a forecast tell us?
choices: What the weather was last year
What the weather will probably be
check.why: A forecast is what scientists think the weather will be.

check.q: In a tornado drill, where do you go?
choices: To a safe hall, away from windows
check.why: A hall with no windows is safer. We crouch and cover our heads.

check.q: Why do forecasts matter?
check.why: A forecast gives people time to get ready for big weather.

lessons.title: Dress for the Day
lessons.mainIdea: We check the weather and choose clothes that keep us safe and comfortable.
reading: Before you go out, check the weather. Cold and snowy? Wear a coat, hat, mittens and boots. Rainy? Bring a *raincoat* and an umbrella. Hot and sunny? Wear light clothes and a hat.
Clothes are like tools. A coat traps warm air near your body. A raincoat keeps water out. A hat keeps sun off your face.
The chart can help you pick. If it has snowed all week, you will probably need boots again. Looking at patterns helps you plan.

words.d: a coat made of a material that does not let water through

look.title: Two Kids at the Door
look.text: It is 30 degrees and snowing. Lily has a coat, mittens and boots. Max has a T-shirt and sandals. They both step outside. After two minutes, one of them runs back in.
look.prompt: Who ran back inside? What should Max wear instead?

check.q: It is snowing. What should you wear?
check.why: Snow means cold. A coat, hat and boots keep you warm and dry.

check.q: What does a raincoat do?
check.why: A raincoat is made of a material that water cannot get through.

check.q: How can the weather chart help you pick clothes?
choices: It picks your clothes for you
Patterns help you guess what is coming
check.why: If it snowed all week, it may snow again. Patterns help you plan.

choices: What the air is like right now
What day of the week it is
review.why: Weather is what the air outside is like today.

review.q: Which tool measures how hot or cold the air is?
review.why: A thermometer gives the temperature as a number.
The seasons go winter, spring, summer, fall.

review.q: Why do we count the stickers on the weather chart?
review.why: Counting turns looking into numbers, and numbers show patterns.

review.q: When does Chicago have the most daylight?
review.why: June has about 15 hours of daylight. December has about 9.

review.q: A tornado warning comes. What is the safe thing to do?
choices: Go to a safe hall and cover your head
review.why: Away from windows, low down, head covered. That is the drill.
